lessons.subject: Engineering Graphics and Design
lessons.title: One object. Three connected views.

reference.title: DBE CAPS Grades 10–12 — Engineering Graphics and Design
reference.note: Teacher must confirm the current annual teaching plan and specialisation. Page numbers count the PDF cover.

lessons.concept: The same stepped solid has width 80, depth 50 and maximum height 40 model units; its lower step is 20 high and its tall portion 30 wide. Third-angle arrangement places the top above the front, and the right-side view to the right. The isometric picture shows appearance; the orthographic views preserve face dimensions.
objectives: Match visible edges of a stepped isometric object to its front, top and right-side views.
Distinguish pictorial appearance from dimension-preserving orthographic views.
Explain and use the stated third-angle layout.
Animate native outlines and matching colours to communicate corresponding views.
voices: One stepped object. The isometric picture shows its shape. The front view shows its stepped height.
The top view shows width and depth. Its internal line marks where the height changes.
The right-side view shows depth and height. The horizontal edge separates the two levels.
This is third-angle projection: top above front, right-side on the right. Match every view to the same object.
lessons.technicalExercise: Sketch the three views of this solid before replaying. Then change width to 100 and the tall portion to 40, keeping depth 50, overall height 40 and step height 20. Draw all three updated views; explain which edges move. Teacher checks the drawing before animation.
lessons.creativeExercise: Use the original separate SVG views. Import or replace each through normal Studio Graphics/media controls. Apply blue/front, mint/top and amber/right-side consistently. Build a native draw-on outline for one view using Stroke end 0→100 over 0.8s. Keep third-angle layout. Submit the native project, exact key table and a complete explanation.
questions: Where does the top view go in this stated convention?
Above the front view. This lesson explicitly uses third-angle projection.
Why is there a line at x=30 in the top view?
It marks the visible change from the tall portion to the lower step; it is not a separate slot.
What width does the right-side view show?
The depth, 50 model units; its height is 40. The front view width is 80.
criteria: Correct front, top and right-side geometry and matching dimensions (6).
State third-angle convention and align the views correctly (4).
Explain a new dimension change without relying on colour alone (4).
Accurate native outline timing, readable labels and safe placement (3).
Editable Studio reconstruction and justified technique choices (3).
lessons.limits: Prepared original static isometric/orthographic SVG assets, not Studio CAD, automatic projection, an engineered working drawing or a rendered 3D scene. Model units are explanatory; no manufacturing dimensions or SANS compliance certification is claimed.

demoControl.reason: Draw attention to a corresponding view without moving or distorting its technical geometry.

lessons.subject: Mechanical Technology
lessons.title: Two gears. One clear ratio.
lessons.grade: Grade 10 systems and control; Grades 11–12 extension

reference.title: DBE CAPS Grades 10–12 — Mechanical Technology
reference.note: Teacher must confirm the current annual teaching plan and specialisation. Page numbers count the PDF cover.

lessons.concept: Two external spur gears have equal module and pressure angle, with 20 driver teeth and 40 driven teeth. Pitch radii are 72 and 144 drawing pixels, fixed centre distance 216. For ideal rolling at the pitch circles, n₁z₁=n₂z₂ and θ₂=−θ₁/2 plus the initial tooth phase. The larger gear turns in the opposite direction at half the speed. A reduction transmits power and ideally increases torque; losses reduce output power.
objectives: Use tooth counts to calculate a 2:1 speed reduction.
Predict opposite directions for two external gears.
Relate reduced speed and increased ideal torque without claiming energy creation.
Build constant-rate native rotation using linear keys and fixed centres.
voices: The small gear is the driver: twenty teeth. It transfers motion through the meshing teeth.
The driven gear has forty teeth. It rotates in the opposite direction. Watch the coloured index dots.
Forty divided by twenty is two. One driver turn produces half a driven turn: half the rotational speed.
Gears transmit mechanical power. Ideally, lower speed gives higher torque. Real friction causes losses; power is not created.
lessons.technicalExercise: Predict direction and turns for a 20-tooth driver and 40-tooth driven gear. Calculate output speed for 120 revolutions per minute input. Then consider a 30-tooth driven gear: state the new ratio, direction, output speed and required pitch-centre distance for drawing module 7.2 pixels.
lessons.creativeExercise: Recreate the two supplied original gear SVGs as separate native image layers. Set centres to (470,350) and (686,350) pixels; preserve dimensions and aspect. Use the key table to complete one full driver turn and half an opposite driven turn over 20 seconds. Do not ease constant-speed rotation. Explain why independent arbitrary spins would mislead a learner.
questions: If the driver turns clockwise, what does the driven gear do?
Counterclockwise, because these are two external gears in direct mesh.
What is the output speed for a 120 rpm input?
Does twice the ideal torque create extra power?
No. Ideal power is torque × angular speed: doubling torque while halving speed preserves power. Friction reduces actual output.
For a 30-tooth driven gear at drawing module 7.2, what changes?
Output is 80 rpm for 120 rpm input, ratio 1.5:1, opposite direction. Pitch radii 72 and 108 give centre distance 180 drawing pixels. New geometry and initial mesh phase are required.
criteria: Identify driver/driven and justify opposing direction (4).
Correct ratio, turn counts and 120→60 rpm calculation (6).
Explain ideal power/torque and real losses (4).
Maintain native fixed centres, correct tooth phase and linear rates (3).
Recreate/edit the project and explain a new gear pair (3).
lessons.limits: Illustrative planar kinematics using prepared original 20° involute SVG contours. Native Studio supplies layer rotation, not gear simulation, contact forces, material stress or manufacturing CAD. Root transitions are simplified, not a cutter/fabrication profile. Drawing pixels are not engineering module in millimetres. Physical angular speed is deliberately slowed for teaching; no real motor is simulated.

demoControl.reason: A complete 360° driver interval corresponds to an opposite 180° driven interval. Linear interpolation preserves the fixed ratio.

lessons.subject: Electrical Technology
lessons.title: Close the path. Light the load.

reference.title: DBE CAPS Grades 10–12 — Electrical Technology
reference.note: Teacher must confirm the current annual teaching plan and specialisation. Page numbers count the PDF cover.

lessons.concept: A low-voltage DC source supplies potential difference; conductors, a switch and a suitable lamp form a series path. Opening the switch breaks the path and the lamp is off. Closing it completes the path and permits current. Conventional current is shown through the external circuit from positive to negative; this is distinct from electron drift in metal. Moving indicators communicate direction, not measured current or the speed of electrons.
objectives: Identify source, conductor, switch and load in a simple DC schematic.
Predict lamp state for open and closed paths.
Trace conventional current through the external circuit from positive to negative.
Distinguish an illustrative animation from an electrical calculation or simulation.
Coordinate switch rotation, lamp opacity and current-marker position keys.
voices: A three-volt source, conductors, a switch and a lamp form a simple circuit. The open switch breaks the path.
Close the switch. The conducting path is complete, so the lamp can light.
The moving indicators show conventional current: from positive, through the external circuit, back to negative. They are not electrons.
Open the switch again: the lamp goes off. This is an illustration, not a simulation. Practical work needs teacher supervision.
lessons.technicalExercise: Draw and label the source, switch, conductors and lamp. Predict lamp state before and after closing the switch. Trace conventional current only in the external circuit. Explain why the animation does not measure current, voltage, electron speed or lamp suitability. No physical wiring is required.
lessons.creativeExercise: Use separate native switch, lamp-light and indicator layers. Close the switch from −35° to 0° at 8.5–9.5s, switch the light on only at closure, and keep indicators inside 10–24s. Open at 24–25s and switch off as contact is broken. Add an original label that distinguishes conventional current from electrons.
questions: Why is the lamp off with the switch open?
The conducting loop is interrupted. In this elementary ideal DC illustration, no steady current flows through the lamp.
Which way is conventional current shown?
From the positive terminal through the external circuit and load to the negative terminal. Electron drift in metal is opposite.
Do the moving dots measure current or electron speed?
No. Their speed and spacing are visual teaching choices. A simulation or measurement would require a circuit model and component values.
criteria: Correct component identification and open/closed reasoning (6).
Correct conventional current direction and distinction from electrons (6).
Clear simulation/supervision limits (2).
Switch/light/marker timings remain causally consistent (3).
Editable project, exact native controls and justified visual choices (3).
lessons.limits: Illustrative low-voltage DC schematic, not an electrical solver or practical wiring plan. 3V is an example source label; component ratings/current are not calculated. No mains activity or unsupervised workshop task. Any real practical must use teacher-approved components and direct supervision.

demoControl.reason: The switch must actually touch the contact before the load is shown as on. The marker communicates direction only.

lessons.subject: Civil Technology
lessons.title: Build the bond, course by course.

reference.title: DBE CAPS Grades 10–12 — Civil Technology
reference.note: Teacher must confirm the current annual teaching plan and specialisation. Page numbers count the PDF cover.

lessons.concept: A cropped front elevation illustrates four stretcher-bond courses. Bed joints separate courses horizontally; vertical perp joints separate adjacent bricks. Alternate courses are offset by half the brick-plus-joint module so their vertical joints do not align. The wall continues beyond both cropped edges. A prepared base and a schematic damp-proof course are contextual layers, not a foundation or waterproofing specification.
objectives: Identify courses, horizontal bed joints and vertical perp joints.
Explain the half-module stagger in stretcher bond.
Sequence the courses from the prepared support upward.
Distinguish a cropped elevation from an end/corner construction detail.
Use native layers, group masking and eased vertical/opacity keys to reveal a sequence.
voices: Start at the prepared support. The dark strip marks a schematic damp-proof course. This is a cropped elevation.
Lay the first stretcher course in the illustration. Mortar forms horizontal bed joints and vertical perp joints.
Offset the next course by half a module. The vertical joints are staggered rather than stacked.
Continue upward, checking the illustrated level and plumb guides. The wall extends beyond the crop. Real construction needs supervised practical training.
lessons.technicalExercise: Draw a three-course cropped stretcher-bond elevation. Mark a bed joint and a perp joint, and explain why alternate joints are staggered. Predict which next-course pattern follows. Explain why cropped edge fragments do not specify cut-brick sizes, corner bonding, foundations or safe construction.
lessons.creativeExercise: Import the four original course assets as separate ordinary image layers. Offset alternate patterns by 80 drawing pixels for the 160-pixel module. Use a native group polygon mask to crop the continuous wall. Reveal courses from bottom to top with Y and opacity keys; add native level/plumb annotations without claiming a site measurement.
questions: What is a bed joint?
The horizontal mortar joint between courses. A perp joint is vertical between neighbouring bricks.
How far is the pattern offset?
Half the brick-plus-joint module: 80 drawing pixels for this 160-pixel module. These are illustration units, not a site dimension specification.
Are the cropped end fragments instructions for half-brick cuts?
No. They show a wall continuing beyond the displayed crop. End/corner details and actual cutting/bonding require the teacher’s technical drawing and supervised instruction.
criteria: Correctly label courses, bed joints and perp joints (6).
Predict alternating half-module stagger and explain its purpose (6).
State crop/base/DPC and practical limits (2).
Correct native layer order, mask and course timings (3).
Recreate an editable sequence and justify the motion/annotation choices (3).
lessons.limits: Supplementary front-elevation illustration, not structural design, a construction method statement or an alternative to supervised workshop training. No real dimensions, mortar mix, load capacity, foundation specification or DPC installation detail is supplied. The colour strip only identifies a contextual DPC layer. Cropped fragments continue outside the frame.

demoControl.reason: The course settles onto the previous bed joint. The shared native polygon mask clips a continuing wall, rather than inventing end-brick sizes.

studioSteps.title: Upload the original stage
studioSteps.control: Workspace → Viral Clip Studio → Choose videos → Open Creator Studio
studioSteps.value: source.mp4 · 1280×720 · 28 seconds · original offline synthetic narration
studioSteps.why: The source is a plain stage with sound. It contains no animated teaching diagrams.

studioSteps.title: Keep the whole composition visible
studioSteps.control: After → Preview quality; Reframe; View options; Sound; Captions
studioSteps.value: Full; 16:9; Show Everyone; Fit full; main frame off; Rounded off; keep original audio; voice repair off; captions off
studioSteps.why: Preserve precise drawing relationships and a stable full-frame lesson.

studioSteps.title: Import the editable scaffold
studioSteps.control: Graphics → Import animated graphics → Import graphics composition…
studioSteps.value: starter.graphics.json; native text, artwork, masks and motion keys
studioSteps.why: Static original SVGs become ordinary editable image layers. Existing keys use the canonical Studio animation graph; they are not an external movie.

studioSteps.title: Complete the key deliberately
studioSteps.control: Motion → Transform keyframes → Target layer → Motion value curve editor → Curve keyframe → Selected motion key value
studioSteps.value: Course 2; y at 8.9s = 63.888889; easing ease_out
studioSteps.why: The course settles onto the previous bed joint. The shared native polygon mask clips a continuing wall, rather than inventing end-brick sizes.

studioSteps.title: Inspect the matching layer or group
studioSteps.control: Composite → Graphic groups → Wall crop → Enable group mask / Mask shape / Polygon path
studioSteps.why: Toggle the native group mask off and on to show the continuing courses, then restore the exact crop. Edge fragments are not prescribed cutting sizes.

studioSteps.title: Add your own annotation
studioSteps.control: Graphics → Add title layer → Label; Copy/time/size; Motion → Transform keyframes → Target layer = Predict first → X/Y
studioSteps.value: Practice label: Predict first; start24s; duration4s; size0.55; width60%; explicitly select Predict first in Target layer; X50 Y84. Remove the practice label before final save.
studioSteps.why: Graphics selection and Motion target are separate. Confirm the new title before editing X/Y so the technical diagram layers remain fixed.

studioSteps.title: Save, export and reopen
studioSteps.control: Show media → Project name → Save; Export → Render Final Clip; Show Finished Video; saved project
studioSteps.value: Unique project name; 720p; 24 fps; original audio; normal local CPU render/download; complete 28s playback; cold reopen
studioSteps.why: The actual authored graph must supply the final result and restore through normal Studio controls.
